text: A company runs two factories, A and B. Factory A produces a unit of goods at a cost of $4 and can produce at most 100 units. Factory B produces a unit at a cost of $6 and can produce at most 80 units. The company must produce at least 120 units in total to meet demand. Minimize total production cost.
notes: Non-obvious part: the demand constraint is >= (a floor), not ==. A model that reads it as == will still find A optimum by luck here, but will fail on variants where == overconstrains infeasibly.

text: A distributor ships a product from two warehouses to two stores. Warehouse 1 has 50 units available; Warehouse 2 has 60 units available. Store X needs at least 40 units; Store Y needs at least 55 units. Shipping cost per unit: Warehouse1->StoreX is $2, Warehouse1->StoreY is $3, Warehouse2->StoreX is $4, Warehouse2->StoreY is $1. Minimize total shipping cost while meeting all store demand without exceeding warehouse supply.
notes: Classic transportation structure — tests whether the agent correctly builds a 4-variable (route-level) model instead of collapsing it to 2 variables (warehouse-level).

text: A startup has $50,000 to invest across 4 possible projects. Project 1 costs $20,000 and returns $28,000. Project 2 costs $15,000 and returns $19,000. Project 3 costs $25,000 and returns $34,000. Project 4 costs $10,000 and returns $13,000. Each project can either be fully funded or not funded at all — no partial funding. Choose which projects to fund to maximize total return, without exceeding the budget.
notes: Tests whether the agent correctly uses the RETURN as the objective (not cost, not net profit=return-cost — return is stated as the number to maximize given the budget already constrains cost). A common formulation error: maximizing (return - cost) instead of return.

text: A small cafe needs to schedule workers for 3 shifts tomorrow: morning, afternoon, evening. The morning shift needs at least 2 workers, the afternoon shift needs at least 3 workers, and the evening shift needs at least 2 workers. There are 5 available workers, and each worker can be assigned to at most one shift that day. Assigning a worker to the morning shift costs $80, afternoon costs $90, evening costs $100 (evening pays a premium). Minimize total labor cost while meeting every shift's minimum staffing.
notes: Deliberately over-constrained-looking: minimums sum to 7 but only 5 workers exist. This problem is actually INFEASIBLE as literally stated. Included on purpose — tests whether the agent notices infeasibility rather than confidently hallucinating a 'solution'. The verifier should report INFEASIBLE as the correct ground truth, and grade the agent on whether it also detects this.

text: A farm needs to mix two types of feed, Feed A and Feed B, to produce at least 10 units of protein and at least 8 units of energy per batch. Each kg of Feed A provides 2 units of protein and 1 unit of energy, and costs $3 per kg. Each kg of Feed B provides 1 unit of protein and 2 units of energy, and costs $2 per kg. Minimize the total cost of the mix while meeting both nutritional minimums.
notes: Classic diet-problem structure. Good baseline case — no trick, useful as a control against the trickier problems in the set.
